parts.name: a "T cells" gate matching the true T cells (F1)

runs.reply:
I set up the T-cell gating and named the final population "T cells". In D01_Unstim, 11,840 of 30,000 events are T cells, which is **39.47% of all events**.

The gating path:

| Gate | Plot and rule | Events | % of parent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lymphocytes | FSC-A × SSC-A, a polygon around the main low-scatter cluster | 19,542 | 65.1% |
| Single cells | FSC-A × FSC-H, automatic singlet gate (area-to-height ratio) | 19,090 | 97.7% |
| Live | Viability (BV510) below 2,500 | 18,776 | 98.4% |
| T cells | CD3 (BV605) at least 3,000 | 11,840 | 63.1% |

The populations were clearly separated in this sample. Dead cells sit near 10⁴ on the viability dye, and the CD3+ cells are around 3×10⁴, well apart from the CD3− cells below 10³. So small changes to the cut-offs would barely change the result.

The gates are still proposals for you to review in CytoWeave. They apply to every sample, but I only checked how well they fit D01_Unstim.

ANSWER: {"percent": 39.47}

parts.name: the wrong entry (APC into Alexa Fluor 700)

runs.reply:
I checked the cytometer's spillover matrix (stored in the stained samples' FCS files) against the 14 single-stain controls. One value is clearly wrong: **APC spilling into the Alexa Fluor 700 detector**.

- **In the file's matrix:** 10.98%
- **What the APC (CD8) control shows:** about 15.8%

So the matrix under-compensates this pair by about 4.8 percentage points. APC-bright cells (CD8+) will look falsely positive for CD4 in the Alexa Fluor 700 channel. Expect a smeared diagonal on CD4 vs CD8 plots, or an inflated CD4+CD8+ population.

No other entry is off by a meaningful amount. The next largest gap is BV605 into BV650 (18.39% vs 18.18%), which is negligible.

The viability control (BV510-A) was brighter in several detectors at once. That's normal for a heat-killed cell control: the dead cells are more autofluorescent. It isn't a spillover error and doesn't change this result.

I haven't changed anything in the workspace. To fix it, either set APC → Alexa Fluor 700-A to about 15.8%, or build a new matrix from the controls (the `propose_compensation` tool does this) and apply it to the stained samples.

ANSWER: {"from": "APC-A", "into": "Alexa Fluor 700-A", "correctPercent": 15.8}

Two other findings, neither a spillover error:

- **BV510 control:** its positive cells are brighter than its negatives in several detectors at once. Spillover doesn't explain that; it looks like autofluorescence, as you'd see in a viability-dye control.

I haven't changed anything in the workspace. To fix the compensation, I can run `propose_compensation` to build a new matrix from the controls for you to review, or you can change that one value to 15.8% yourself.

parts.name: the wrong entry (APC into Alexa Fluor 700)

runs.reply:
I checked the matrix stored in the files ($SPILLOVER, which the stained samples use) against the 14 single-stain controls. The wrong value is **APC into Alexa Fluor 700**: the matrix has **10.98%**, and the APC (CD8) bead control shows it should be about **15.8%**.

- **What happens with the current value:** about 4.8 points of APC signal stays in the Alexa Fluor 700 channel (CD4) after compensation. CD8⁺ cells would therefore look falsely CD4-dim or positive, and the CD4⁺CD8⁺ double-positive gate would be inflated.
- **Every other value is close to what the controls give.** The next largest gap is BV605 into BV650: 18.39% in the file against 18.18% from the controls. That 0.2-point difference is within noise.
- **The viability (BV510) control** is brighter in several detectors at once. That isn't a spillover error: the control is half heat-killed cells, and dead cells are more autofluorescent. Its matrix values look fine.

I haven't changed anything in the workspace. To fix it, you can edit that single value to 15.8%, or have CytoWeave compute a new matrix from the controls and accept it.

ANSWER: {"from": "APC-A", "into": "Alexa Fluor 700-A", "correctPercent": 15.8}

Stimulation increases the percentage of CD25+ cells among CD4 T cells. It goes from a mean of 7.3% unstimulated to 33.3% stimulated, and the paired t-test gives p = 8.7 × 10⁻⁹.

**Gating.** I used the existing path down to T cells (Cells / Single cells / Live / Lymphocytes / T cells) and added two gates under it. Both are proposals waiting for your review in the window:
- **CD4 T cells:** a rectangle on CD4 against CD8, taking CD4 from 3,000 to 50,000 and CD8 from −300 to 1,500. The rectangle's lower CD8 edge at −300 may leave out a few CD4 cells with the lowest CD8 values.
- **CD25+:** CD25 (PE) ≥ 2,000. That threshold is just above the unstimulated cells' CD25-negative cloud, and the same gate is used on every sample. I set it by eye from donor D01's plots and didn't run a check of how much the result depends on the exact threshold.

**Test.** Each donor was measured both unstimulated and stimulated, so I compared condition paired by donor, with one value per sample.

| Donor | Unstimulated | Stimulated |
|---|---|---|
| D01 | 9.5 | 35.7 |
| D02 | 5.6 | 32.5 |
| D03 | 10.6 | 35.2 |
| D04 | 5.8 | 32.1 |
| D05 | 5.4 | 30.6 |
| D06 | 7.0 | 33.4 |

- **Paired t-test:** the mean increase is 25.9 percentage points (95% CI 25.0 to 26.8), t(5) = 73.7, **p = 8.7 × 10⁻⁹**.
- **Wilcoxon signed-rank test (exact):** p = 0.031. With only six donors, this is the smallest p-value this test can give, because all six donors went up.

ANSWER: {"direction": "up", "p": 8.68804e-9}

Yes. Stimulation raises the percentage of CD25+ cells among CD4 T cells. It went up in all six donors, by about 26 percentage points on average, and the paired t-test gives p = 8.7 × 10⁻⁹.

**Gating:** I used the existing tree down to T cells (Cells, then single cells, live cells, lymphocytes and CD3+ T cells) and added two gates:
- **CD4 T cells:** a rectangle on CD4 vs CD8 (CD4 3,500–50,000, CD8 below 2,000) that excludes the CD8 T cells. One donor, D04, scored as an outlier at about 47% CD4. I looked at its plot and the gate fits; that donor simply has more CD8 cells, in both conditions.
- **CD25+:** CD25 (PE) ≥ 2,000. That threshold sits just above the end of the CD25-negative cloud in the unstimulated sample and below the CD25+ cells.

Both gates are waiting for you to accept them in CytoWeave.

| Donor | Unstimulated | Stimulated |
|---|---|---|
| D01 | 9.5% | 35.7% |
| D02 | 5.6% | 32.5% |
| D03 | 10.6% | 35.2% |
| D04 | 5.8% | 32.1% |
| D05 | 5.4% | 30.6% |
| D06 | 7.0% | 33.4% |
| **Mean** | **7.3%** | **33.2%** |

**Test:** Each donor was measured in both conditions, so I paired the samples by donor and used a two-sided paired t-test.
- The mean increase is 25.9 points (95% CI 25.0–26.8), with t(5) = −73.6 and p = 8.7 × 10⁻⁹.
- A Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a check gives p = 0.031. With only six pairs, that is the smallest p-value this test can produce, and every donor went up.

The exact percentages depend on where the CD25 threshold sits; the review rated it robust for D01 and D03 stimulated and moderately sensitive for the other samples. I didn't run a formal robustness check, but the gap between conditions is far larger than any reasonable shift of the threshold would change.

ANSWER: {"direction": "up", "p": 8.74e-9}

Yes. Stimulation raises the percentage of CD25+ cells among CD4 T cells, and the increase is very large.

**What I gated:** I used the existing Cells → Single cells → Live → Lymphocytes → T cells gates. Under T cells I added two gates:
- **CD4 T cells:** a rectangle on CD4 against CD8, taking CD4 from 3,000 to 50,000 and CD8 from −300 to 1,000.
- **CD25+:** CD25 (PE-A) above 2,000. I set this cutoff above the main CD25-negative cloud of the unstimulated sample. The same cutoff applies to all 12 samples, with no per-sample adjustment, so they are measured the same way.

I only looked at plots from D01 and D04, not every sample. Both gates are still proposals in the window, waiting for you to accept or reject them.

**Results (% CD25+ of CD4 T cells):**

| Donor | Unstimulated | Stimulated |
|---|---|---|
| D01 | 9.5 | 35.7 |
| D02 | 5.6 | 32.5 |
| D03 | 10.6 | 35.2 |
| D04 | 5.8 | 32.1 |
| D05 | 5.4 | 30.6 |
| D06 | 7.0 | 33.4 |
| **Mean** | **7.3** | **33.3** |

**Test:** Each donor was measured both ways, so I used a paired t-test with donors as the pairs. The mean increase is 25.9 percentage points (95% CI 25.0 to 26.8), with t(5) = 73.7 and **p = 8.7 × 10⁻⁹**. Every donor went up.

As a cross-check, the exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p = 0.031. That is the smallest p-value this test can give with 6 pairs, so it agrees with the t-test.

The result depends on where the CD25 cutoff sits, but I didn't test other cutoffs. The gap between groups is large and the same in every donor, so moving the cutoff a little is unlikely to change the conclusion.

ANSWER: {"direction": "up", "p": 8.68804e-9}

I ran acquisition QC (PeacoQC plus flow-rate, margin and drift checks) on all four wells. For A04 I also plotted signal against time to check what QC found. A01 is the only clean acquisition.

| Well | QC score | What went wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **A01** | 100 (good) | Nothing. Only 10 of 40,000 events were flagged (0.03%), and no channel drifted. |
| **A02** | 82 | **Clog.** The flow rate dropped at about 8–11 s, which is what a partial clog does. QC removed 3,005 events (7.5%). The rest of the run is stable and no channel drifted. |
| **A03** | 80 | **Drift.** Every fluorescence channel lost signal steadily from the start to the end of the run, for example BV605 (CD3) −40%, BV786 (CD45) −38%, BV510 −33% and BV711 −29%. The flow rate stayed steady and almost no events were flagged, so the problem is a loss of signal over time, not a flow problem. Removing events won't fix it, so treat this file's intensities with caution. |
| **A04** | 44 (poor) | **Air bubble.** At about 12–13 s there is a short burst of events with low scatter and fluorescence: FSC-H falls and some events hit the top of the scale. QC removed 9,613 events (24%). QC also reported a −23% "drift" in BV605. The time plot shows this comes from the bubble's events dragging the signal down at that one point. Before and after the bubble, the CD3 levels are flat. |

The QC results and a "QC pass" channel are waiting for your review in CytoWeave. If you accept them, you can gate on that channel to drop the flagged events from A02 and A04. A03 needs to be re-acquired or normalised instead.

ANSWER: {"A01": "clean", "A02": "clog", "A03": "drift", "A04": "bubble"}

I ran acquisition QC (refined PeacoQC, flow rate, margin events and per-channel drift) on all four wells, then plotted the flagged ones against time to check what QC found.

- **A01 is clean.** It scored 100 out of 100. The flow rate and signals are steady, and only 10 of 40,000 events were flagged.
- **A02 has a clog.** The event rate drops to near zero around 8–11 s, then surges to about twice the normal rate as the clog clears. After that it returns to its steady level. The fluorescence signals are stable. 7.5% of events fall in the affected stretch.
- **A03 has signal drift.** The flow is steady and almost no events were removed. But every fluorescence channel loses intensity over the run, by roughly 30–40% from start to end (for example CD3 BV605 −40%, CD45 BV786 −38%, Viability BV510 −33%). You can see the CD3+ band sloping down over time, which points to a slow instrument or laser change rather than a fluidics event. You can't fix this by removing events, so treat this well's intensities (MFIs) with caution.
- **A04 has an air bubble.** At about 12–13 s there's a short burst of events with collapsed FSC-H and a scatter of saturated values. QC removed 24% of events, and the score was 44 ("poor"). QC also reported a −23% "drift" in CD3 BV605. The plot shows that comes only from the bubble's low events; the CD3+ band is flat on either side of it, so it isn't real drift.

The QC result, including a "QC pass" channel, is waiting for your review in CytoWeave. You can gate on that channel to drop the bad stretches in A02 and A04.

ANSWER: {"A01": "clean", "A02": "clog", "A03": "drift", "A04": "bubble"}

I ran acquisition QC on all four acquisitions (PeacoQC, plus checks on flow rate, margin events and signal drift). Only A01 is clean; the other three each had a different problem.

| Sample | Score | Verdict | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A01** | 100 (good) | **Clean** | No findings: flow rate and signal were stable, and only 10 of 40,000 events (0.03%) were flagged. |
| **A02** | 82 | **Clog** | The flow rate dropped between 8 and 11 s, which is what a partial clog does. QC removed 7.5% of events. The fluorescence channels didn't drift. |
| **A03** | 80 | **Drift** | Signal fell steadily from start to end in 7 channels: BV510 −33%, BV605 −40%, BV711 −29%, BV786 −38%, and PerCP-Cy5.5, APC and Alexa Fluor 700 also dropped. Event flow was fine (only 3 events removed). The score is still "acceptable" only because removing events can't fix a slow drift. Medians or % positive from this file will be biased. |
| **A04** | 44 (poor) | **Bubble** | At 12–13 s the FSC-H signal dropped and a burst of events came through, which is an air bubble (or debris) passing through. QC removed 24% of events. BV605 also fell 23% over the run; I think that's minor next to the bubble, but I didn't check whether it's real. |

The QC results are only proposed for now. If you accept them, a "QC pass" channel is added that you can gate on to keep the good events in A02 and A04. A03 can't be fixed that way, so I'd re-acquire it or leave it out of anything that depends on intensity.

parts.detail: Clog: the flow rate dropped (partial blockage) partway through acquisition, about 5–7 s, followed by a surge and a debris streak as it cleared; QC removed about 8% of events

answer.problem: Clog: the flow rate dropped (partial blockage) partway through acquisition, about 5–7 s, followed by a surge and a debris streak as it cleared; QC removed about 8% of events

runs.reply:
The sample with the problem is **D05_Unstim**: a **clog (partial blockage of the fluidics) partway through acquisition**.

I ran acquisition QC on all twelve stained samples and then looked at plots against acquisition time:

- **Flow rate:** The event rate is steady at about 900 events per bin until roughly 5–7 s. It then falls to about a third of that, followed by a surge to over 1,000 when the flow resumes. That pattern is what a clog that clears looks like.
- **Scatter:** On Time vs FSC-A there's a gap at that point and then a narrow streak of low-FSC events where the flow restarts, which is debris or doublets coming through as the clog cleared.
- **Effect:** QC flagged about 8% of its events (2,407 of 30,000) for removal and gave it a score of 81. The other ten samples scored 100 and lost about 0.03% of their events or less.

The only other flag was a −17% drift in the BV650 (HLA-DR) channel over D04_Unstim's run (score 95). It isn't visible on the Time vs HLA-DR plot and there's no flow problem with it, so I don't consider it an acquisition fault.

The QC results are waiting for your review in CytoWeave. If you accept them, the flagged clog events in D05_Unstim can be gated out using the "QC pass" channel.

ANSWER: {"sample": "D05_Unstim", "problem": "Clog: the flow rate dropped (partial blockage) partway through acquisition, about 5–7 s, followed by a surge and a debris streak as it cleared; QC removed about 8% of events"}

parts.name: the cause (a degraded tandem)
parts.detail: Tandem dye degradation: the PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has broken down more than in its single-stain reference control (≈11.5% extra emission as PE, e.g. from light/heat/fixation/time), so the reference spectrum doesn't match and PE-Cy7 signal leaks into PE

answer.cause: Tandem dye degradation: the PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has broken down more than in its single-stain reference control (≈11.5% extra emission as PE, e.g. from light/heat/fixation/time), so the reference spectrum doesn't match and PE-Cy7 signal leaks into PE

runs.reply:
e unmixing diagnosis on each donor, and every one gave the same single high‑confidence finding:
- **The pattern:** in all three donors, PE's negative population rises in step with PE‑Cy7 brightness. The slope is 0.115 units of PE per unit of PE‑Cy7 (z ≈ 860–940). About 66–68% of PE‑Cy7‑positive events sit on that diagonal, against about 0.01% on a flat line. Across PE‑Cy7's range this moves PE up by about 25–27 noise SDs.
- **What it means:** when a PE‑Cy7 tandem breaks down, some of its light comes out as PE instead. In the donors, PE‑Cy7 gives off about 11.5% more of its light as PE than its reference control did. The reference spectrum therefore doesn't match the dye in the samples, so CD45‑bright cells get false PE signal and look falsely CD25‑positive.
- **Why the residual stays low:** the misplaced light has the shape of PE, which the model already includes, so it lands in the PE channel instead of the residual. You see it as a diagonal on a PE‑Cy7 vs PE plot.
- **Why it's the sample, not the control:** the effect is the same in all three donors. Other possible leaks were each flagged as having no consensus (BV650→BV421 and PE‑Cy5→PE in all three donors, the others in some), and they varied between donors. The usual reasons a tandem degrades in the samples but not the control are light exposure, heat, fixation, or time between staining the control and staining the samples.

**Fix:** the best fix is a new PE‑Cy7 reference control stained from the same vial at the same time as the samples. Short of that, the Spectral view's Diagnose tab offers a stopgap: swap in the PE‑Cy7 spectrum the samples show (adding the extra 11.5% PE), then unmix again. I haven't applied either.

ANSWER: {"dye": "PE-Cy7", "cause": "Tandem dye degradation: the PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has broken down more than in its single-stain reference control (≈11.5% extra emission as PE, e.g. from light/heat/fixation/time), so the reference spectrum doesn't match and PE-Cy7 signal leaks into PE"}

runs.reply:
pulation rises with it, at about **0.115 PE per unit of PE-Cy7** in S1, S2 and S3 (z ≈ 860–940).
  - About two-thirds of the PE-Cy7-positive cells sit on that diagonal, against about 0.01% if there were no leak. Across PE-Cy7's range this moves PE by roughly 25 noise SDs.
  - So in the samples, PE-Cy7 gives off about **11.5% more of its light as PE** than its control did. That's what happens when a tandem degrades: the Cy7 acceptor stops taking up the energy and the PE donor gives it off itself.
- Other causes look unlikely:
  - No light was left unexplained, so no dye is missing a reference.
  - The Unstained control covers about 99.8% of the donor cells, so autofluorescence is accounted for.
  - The other possible tandem leaks either weren't consistent across checks or were small.

The residuals stay low because the light that leaks out is PE's own spectrum, which the model already contains. It goes wrong silently: the donor samples get false CD25 (PE) signal on CD45-bright cells, and their CD45 is slightly understated.

**Likely cause and fix:** the PE-Cy7 used on the donors broke down more than the vial used for the reference control. Light, heat, fixation or time between staining the control and the samples can each do this. The best fix is a new PE-Cy7 single-stain control, stained from the same vial at the same time as the samples. A quicker fallback is in the Spectral view's Diagnose tab: replace the PE-Cy7 reference with the spectrum the samples show (PE-Cy7 plus 11.5% PE), then unmix again.

The unmixing and its reference library are proposed in the workspace and are waiting for you to review them.

answer.cause: Tandem dye degradation: the PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain reference control (light, heat, fixation or time), so it emits about 11.5% more as PE, and unmixing puts false PE signal on PE-Cy7-positive cells

runs.reply:
the PE-negative cells (CD25) rise with it: about 0.115 units of PE for every unit of PE-Cy7.
- About two-thirds of the PE-Cy7-positive events sit on that diagonal, against about 0.01% on a flat line. Across PE-Cy7's range the shift is about 25–27 noise SDs (z ≈ 860–940).
- The residual stays low because the extra light is PE's emission, which is already in the model. So unmixing assigns it to PE instead of leaving it unexplained.
- CD45 is on every leukocyte, so this puts false CD25 (PE) signal on essentially every cell.
- I ruled out the other likely causes:
  - All 25 dyes have a reference, and there is no light the references don't explain.
  - The other tandem pairs (PE-Cy5→PE, BV650→BV421) don't show a leak consistent across donors.
  - The Unstained control covers about 99.8% of the donors' cells, and none of the autofluorescence-like dyes rise with autofluorescence.

**Most likely cause:** the PE-Cy7 tandem in the stained donor samples has broken down more than in its bead control. Typical reasons are light exposure, heat, fixation, or time between staining the control and the samples. In the donors it gives off about 11.5% more of its light as PE than the reference does.

**Fix:** the unmixing is only proposed so far; nothing is accepted in the workspace yet. Ideally, re-acquire a PE-Cy7 single-stain control stained from the same vial at the same time as the samples. Otherwise, the Diagnose tab in the Spectral view has a fix that swaps in the PE-Cy7 spectrum the samples actually show. You would apply it there and then unmix again. In the diagnosis's test of that fix, the PE leak dropped to about zero. Until one of these is done, don't trust CD25 (PE) results in CD45-bright cells.

ANSWER: {"dye": "PE-Cy7", "cause": "Tandem dye degradation: the PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain reference control (light, heat, fixation or time), so it emits about 11.5% more as PE, and unmixing puts false PE signal on PE-Cy7-positive cells"}

parts.name: the amount (125 ng: twice the amount near 90% of saturation)

runs.reply:
Use **125 ng of CD4-PE per test.**

**What I did:** I gated the lymphocytes on FSC-A vs SSC-A first, because monocytes carry low CD4 and would blur the positive population. Then I ran the titration on PE-A within that gate, across all 10 two-fold steps from 1.95 to 1000 ng.

| ng/test | Positive median | Negative median | Negative rSD | Stain index |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.95 | 5,583 | 12 | 28 | 101 |
| 7.81 | 12,170 | 12 | 28 | 220 |
| 31.25 | 16,990 | 15 | 28 | 303 |
| 62.5 | 18,300 | 18 | 29 | 311 |
| **125** | **19,310** | **22** | **31** | **313 (highest)** |
| 250 | 19,730 | 33 | 34 | 290 |
| 500 | 19,850 | 52 | 44 | 223 |
| 1000 | 19,960 | 92 | 65 | 152 |

- **Saturation:** the positive (CD4+ T cell) signal levels off at about 19–20k from 125 ng up. A saturation curve fitted to the stain index reaches 90% of its maximum at about 36 ng.
- **Rule for the recommendation:** take the first amount tested at or above twice that 90% point (Bonilla et al. 2024). That is 125 ng.
- **Background:** above 125 ng the CD4− cells pick up non-specific staining. Their median rises from 22 to 92 and their spread doubles, so the stain index falls to 152 at 1000 ng. More antibody only adds background.
- **Two methods agree:** 125 ng is also where the stain index peaks. If reagent is tight, 62.5 ng gives almost the same separation (stain index 311), but it sits on the slope of the curve, so it is less robust to changes in cell number or staining volume.

The lymphocyte gate and the titration result are proposed in the workspace for you to accept or reject. The tubes named "Voltage walk" weren't part of this question, so I didn't analyze them.

ANSWER: {"amountNg": 125}

parts.name: the amount (125 ng: twice the amount near 90% of saturation)

runs.reply:
Use **125 ng of CD4-PE per test**.

**How I got there:** The FSC/SSC plot showed monocytes, which carry CD4 at low levels, mixed in with the lymphocytes. Their middle peak in PE would have skewed the positive population, so I gated the lymphocytes first. That gate is proposed in the workspace for you to review; it covers 66% of events in the 1000 ng tube. I then ran the titration analysis on PE-A within that gate.

| ng/test | Positive median | Negative median | Negative rSD | Stain index |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.95 | 5,594 | 12 | 27 | 102 |
| 7.81 | 12,190 | 12 | 28 | 220 |
| 31.25 | 17,020 | 15 | 28 | 306 |
| 62.5 | 18,330 | 17 | 29 | 313 |
| **125** | **19,320** | **22** | **31** | **315 (highest)** |
| 250 | 19,740 | 33 | 34 | 293 |
| 500 | 19,860 | 52 | 44 | 225 |
| 1000 | 20,010 | 92 | 65 | 153 |

- **The positive signal levels off:** the positive median barely rises above about 60–125 ng. A saturation curve fitted to the stain index puts 90% of saturation at about 37 ng.
- **Too much antibody adds background:** above 125 ng the negative cells get brighter and more spread out (negative median 22 → 92, rSD 31 → 65), so the stain index drops from 315 to 153 by 1000 ng.
- **Two criteria agree:** 125 ng has the best stain index. It is also what the Bonilla et al. 2024 rule gives: the first amount tested at or above twice the 90%-saturation amount (2 × 37 ≈ 73 ng, so 125 ng).

62.5 ng resolves almost as well (stain index 313) and would save half the antibody. 125 ng is the safer choice because it leaves room for samples with more cells or more CD4. The CD4+ fraction stayed near 50% at every amount, so even the lowest amounts separate the CD4+ cells.

ANSWER: {"amountNg": 125}

parts.name: the inactive compounds (CW-105; CW-106 either way)

runs.reply:
CW-103 is the most potent inhibitor, with an IC50 of about 3.2 nM (95% CI 2.8–3.6 nM). CW-105 is the only compound that shows no inhibition at the doses tested.**

**How I measured it:** I used the existing gates (Lymphocytes → Live → T cells → CD69+) and the %CD69+ of live T cells in each well. The CD69 gate sits in the gap between the negative and positive peaks in both the stimulated (DMSO) and unstimulated controls, so I kept it as it was. The assay window is good: the 18 stimulated controls average 63.4% CD69+ and the 18 unstimulated controls average 3.8%, giving Z′ = 0.84. I converted each well to % inhibition against these controls and fitted a 4-parameter log-logistic curve per compound, with the bottom fixed at 0% and the top at 100%.

| Compound | IC50 (nM) | 95% CI | Hill slope | R² | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CW-103** | **3.2** | 2.8–3.6 | 0.70 | 0.997 | Most potent |
| CW-101 | 27.2 | 26.4–28.1 | 0.97 | 1.000 | Potent |
| CW-102 | 302 | 209–436 | 1.5 | 0.97 | Moderate |
| CW-104 | 1,270 | 559–2,885 | 0.38 | 0.93 | Weak, shallow curve |
| CW-106 | ~17,800 | 7,500–42,250 | 1.1 | 0.76 | Weak; IC50 is beyond the top dose (extrapolated) |
| **CW-105** | — | — | — | 0.13 | **No inhibition** |

- **CW-105:** CD69+ stays at 60–70% at every dose, from 0.5 nM to 10 µM, which is the same as the stimulated controls. The curve fits no better than a flat line (F test p = 0.30).
- **CW-106 (borderline):** it only acts at the top doses. CD69+ is about 57% at 3.3 µM and 43% at 10 µM, roughly 35% inhibition at most. This is statistically real (p = 0.001), so I didn't call it inactive. But it never reaches 50% inhibition on this plate, so its IC50 is only an extrapolation. If you count "no meaningful inhibition" rather than "none at all", you could put CW-106 in that group too.
- **Viability:** the live fraction is 95–97% in every well, so none of the drops in CD69 come from cells dying.

ANSWER: {"mostPotent": "CW-103", "ic50nM": 3.2, "inactive": ["CW-105"]}

I normalised each well to % inhibition against the plate controls: 18 stimulated (DMSO) wells average 63.4% CD69+ and 18 unstimulated wells average 3.8%. The plate's Z′ is 0.84, which is excellent. I checked the CD69+ gate on a stimulated control well and it sits cleanly in the gap between the negative and positive peaks.

| Compound | IC50 (nM) | 95% CI | Hill | R² | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CW-103** | **3.2** | 2.8–3.6 | 0.70 | 0.997 | Most potent; fully inhibits from about 1 µM up |
| CW-101 | 27.2 | 26.4–28.1 | 0.97 | 0.9998 | Fully inhibits |
| CW-102 | 302 | 209–436 | 1.5 | 0.97 | Fully inhibits at high doses |
| CW-104 | ~1,270 | 559–2,885 | 0.38 | 0.93 | Shallow, incomplete curve: only about 55% inhibition at 10 µM |
| CW-106 | >10,000 (fit says ~17,800) | 7,500–42,250 | — | 0.76 | Only the 10 µM well is reduced (42.7% vs about 60% at lower doses). The IC50 lies beyond the highest dose, so it's a weak, extrapolated estimate |
| **CW-105** | — | — | — | 0.13 | No dose–response (no-effect test p = 0.30); 54–70% CD69+ at every dose, the same as stimulated controls |

- **Most potent:** CW-103, IC50 ≈ 3.2 nM.
- **No inhibition at the doses tested:** CW-105.
